extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and principles for construing patent claims, deciding literal and equivalent infringement (especially for chemical/composition patents), and measuring damages for infringement. Covers when substitutions or omissions evade a claim, the role of intent, and the proper measures of actual damages and trebled damages under statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel from expressly waived claim in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the patentee must be held to be estopped from asserting a claim which is expressly waived on the record.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification expressly disclaims a substance or class of use, the patentee cannot later claim that subject-matter; the specification serves to inform the public what may be safely done during the patent term without infringing. (Applied to a patentee who declared his invention 'did not extend to the use' of a particular substance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of a 'new combination' claim excludes use of individual old materials alone
rubrics_metrics.description: 'any one may use any one or all of the materials forming the composition, provided he does not use them in the combination patented.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the patent claims a new combination of previously known ingredients, third parties may lawfully use individual ingredients or other combinations (including the old combination with a formerly essential ingredient) so long as they do not practice the patented combination itself. Infringement inquiry asks whether defendant used the plaintiff's combination 'substantially according to their patent.' (See friction-match examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or insignificance of an omitted ingredient determines infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether defendant's product 'contain[s] that substance as a principal ingredient, in conformity with the prescribed formula, or whether they are made without it or with so inconsiderable a portion of it as to be substantially according to plaintiff's patent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claimed composition omits an ingredient used in prior art, courts look to whether defendants actually include that ingredient (or include it only in trivial amounts) to decide if their product is substantially the patented composition. Factual finding on presence/quantity is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the 'sine qua non' or essence of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: 'What forms the essence or substance of this discovery? What is the sine qua non, or that without which this composition of matter cannot be produced?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the essential element(s) (e.g., a specific temperature range, a particular step, or a component in a particular state). Variations in proportions, substitute materials, or modes of application that nonetheless rely on the patentee's essential discovery may still pirate the invention if they appropriate the patentee's 'platform' or essential principle (examples given in vulcanization and heat application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents applied differently in chemistry than mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I do not quite go along with the doctrine of equivalents in chemistry applied in the same way as in mechanics... in chemistry you almost entirely fail [to predict equivalents]...You cannot anticipate the result; it is a mere question of result upon experiment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In chemistry, 'equivalent' substitutions are empirical and unpredictable; courts are cautious applying mechanical-style equivalence reasoning to chemical processes/compounds. Juries may treat probable anticipations as servile imitation or colorable evasion, but chemical equivalence often requires experiment or proof of equal operation/function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution by a natural or composite article may fall within claims if specification's language so covers it
rubrics_metrics.description: If a defendant uses an article (e.g., borax) which is composed of ingredients the specification claims (acid + alkali), it may be 'exactly the same thing' as claiming the separate ingredients; conversely, if the article is used merely for a different function (e.g., as a flux), that may not be infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the specification's words cover the composite/natural article in substance. If the language 'conveys the same meaning' as describing component acids/alkalies, infringement may be found; but if the article operates in a different way (flux vs acid/alkali role), it may be outside the patent. (Discussed in Martin's cement/borax context.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of patent claims must adhere to what the specification actually explains
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In order to decide this (the infringement), we must first determine for what invention the patent, as explained by the specification, is taken out.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim scope is determined by construing the specification: what the patentee explained and distinguished (e.g., Heath patent limited to 'carburet of manganese' in that state and mode). Courts will not read the claim broader than the invention as described in the specification; differences in wording that nevertheless 'convey the same meaning' may be treated as the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement requires use in the mode described; indirect (colorable) variation depends on substitution of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement: using the substance 'in the mode described in the specification.' Indirect infringement: 'if a defendant substitutes for a part of a plaintiff's invention some well-known equivalent...he would probably be considered as only making a colorable variation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literal (direct) infringement needs the defendant to practice the claimed mode/state. Indirect infringement can exist where a defendant makes a colorable variation by substituting a known equivalent that accomplishes the same result; courts examine whether the substitution was intentionally imitative or effectively the same in result and operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent to imitate is not dispositive of infringement (conflicting views exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Evidence of intention to imitate may be material... but if the invention be in point of fact adopted or imitated, whether in ignorance or intention, the infringement is just the same.' (Contrast with Exchequer's language that absence of intention suggests no imitation.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some authorities treat objective adoption (whether intentional or not) as sufficient for infringement; other decisions have given weight to intent in assessing colorable variations. Practitioners should note both strands: intent can be probative but is not universally required for finding infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a natural product in its natural state may not infringe a patent limited to an artificial product, but processing/revivification can infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: '...the right of the patentee was restricted to the use of artificial precipitated oxides of iron, and that the user by defendants of a natural product known as bog ochre in its natural state...was no infringement; but...the revivification of the natural product was an infringement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the patentee's claim is limited to an artificial/prepared form; if so, mere use of a naturally occurring substance that performs the same function may be noninfringing, whereas applying the patentee's claimed processing (revivification or adaptation) to a natural product can be infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'equivalent' in chemical fluid substitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This term 'equivalent,' when speaking of machines, has a certain definite meaning; but when used with regard to the chemical action of such fluids...it only means equally good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For chemical mixtures or fluids, 'equivalent' should be understood as producing an equally good result (practical equivalence), and attention must be paid to the proportions prescribed in the specification (e.g., equal parts by measure if the specification prescribes that proportion). Expert proof of equal effectiveness is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of 'actual damages' and treble damages statutory rule
rubrics_metrics.description: 'By the terms "actual damages, sustained by the plaintiff," are meant such damages as he can actually prove...These damages will be trebled by the court, according to the statute.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Actual damages' are those the plaintiff can prove he actually sustained (not imaginary/vindicative awards). The statute permits the court to increase damages up to three times actual damages 'according to the circumstances of the case.' Assessors should separate provable actual losses from punitive or speculative amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper measure of actual damages for use-made infringing machines: defendant's actual profits (not hypothetical profits)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In cases of infringement by an actual use of the plaintiff's invention...to give the value of such use during the time of the illegal user, that is to say, the amount of profits actually received by the defendant, but not the profits which he might have made by reasonable diligence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages for unauthorized use of a patented machine are measured by the defendant's profits actually received from the infringing use; courts generally do not award hypothetical profits the defendant might have earned with reasonable efforts. Additionally, addible are 'all the losses to which the plaintiff has been subjected by the piracy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Using the sale/price of the machine as damages is controversial and not generally favored
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It has been maintained...that the price of the invented machine is a proper measure of damages... But the rule itself...has no merit from its universality of application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some argue that the sale price of a machine can measure damages (because a verdict effectively transfers the right), courts warn this can unfairly operate as a forced sale and is problematic where the patentee never sold rights or value depends on limited users. Use profits and provable losses remain the preferred measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where no established patent/license fee exists, evidence of utility and superiority may be admissible to show damages
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Where there is no established patent or license-fee, general evidence of the utility and superiority of the invention may be...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no fixed licensing practice or established royalty, courts may permit general evidence (e.g., market utility, superiority) to help prove the value of the invention and thus the damages sustained from infringement. (Text cuts off but indicates admissibility of such evidence.)
